| [CLAIM-529](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-529.md) v3 | An organization can be individuated without presupposing it as a declared candidate whose verdict can come out false: criteria stated on the candidate's interactions (whether benefit can be booked per member, which interactions the others depend on, what removing an interaction type does, whether its order survives release from an outside scaffold) apply to a grouping not yet assumed to be a unit, while criteria stated as members' attitudes toward the group (a goal about it, belonging, identity) make it partly constituted by being taken as one, individuating it by a different relation, unavailable where members have no such attitudes | Filed on re-reading Griesemer & Shavit 2023 ([LIT-188](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-188.md), [NOTE-173](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-173.md)). Their abstract says transitions in individuality are hard to describe without circularity, since the features used are products of the transition, and claims a non-circular description that the body never argues. The body holds the parts of an answer, and they are of two kinds. Criteria on interactions (per-member accounting of benefit, entrenchment order, knockout of interaction types, release from a scaffold) can test a declared candidate without assuming it is a unit ([CLAIM-405](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-405.md)), and the scaffold test needs the declared boundary ([CLAIM-522](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-522.md)). Criteria on members' attitudes toward the group (shared goal, belonging, focal goal of sustaining it) individuate constitutively, which is not the non-circular route and is unavailable for organisms without such attitudes. It does not say the paper argues this, and it leaves the presupposed lower-level units where the paper leaves them. | Active |
